title: Implicit Self-Evaluations Predict Changes in Implicit Partner Evaluations

selection.evidence: Assigned by mark as item 8 of 8 in a blinded known-answer control of my reading protocol (identifiers only, 2026-10-23T16:11). No prior knowledge of the paper; prior suspicion: none.

cost.compute_notes: NIH author manuscript as JATS from NCBI efetch (Europe PMC fullTextXML HTTP 500). OSF hdi8p .sav + qfgn6 measures acquired with checksums. Python: statsmodels MixedLM random intercept by couple for Tables 2-3, robustness (winsorised, rank, Cook's, leave-one-couple-out), 24-predictor covariate model, null-model fit to the 4x4 correlation matrix + 4,000 simulations, couple-cluster bootstrap of the cross-lagged difference.

triggers: implicit self-esteem predicts change in implicit partner evaluation newlyweds
affective priming test-retest reliability three years
known-answer control psychological science 2014 open data

claims.statement: Newlyweds' baseline implicit self-evaluations positively predict change in their implicit partner evaluations over three years (B = .26, SE = .10, r = .35), controlling baseline implicit partner evaluation; robust to ~20 covariates (B = .30, t(24) = 3.00, p = .006). Explicit self-esteem predicts no change in any interpersonal evaluation.
claims.scope: 104 spouses (56 couples minus exclusions), random intercept by couple, standardised coefficients.

quantities.name: null_model_false_positive_rate
quantities.baseline: stable latent S and P, no effect of S on change, shared session method; median std beta 0.141, 95th pct 0.309 vs observed 0.253

our_assessment.why: Reproduces (B .26 standardised; covariate model p = .003; survives Holm over 6 tests at .043). But it is fragile (rank p = .17; one couple's removal can give p = .19), and residualised change with a baseline retest of ~.2 and a same-session predictor produces this result 28% of the time in a fitted null world with no effect; the cross-lagged asymmetry that would favour direction is not distinguishable from zero. 'Long-awaited evidence' over-states it.

claims.statement: Table 2 prints the implicit-partner three-year mean as 35.67 (62.83), which is the implicit-self value; the deposit gives 32.50 (61.08). The printed change (-16.74) is correct, which exposes the pasted cell. The d column does not follow from the table's own t-values for within-person change (self-esteem d = 1.67 for a 0.09-point change), and several Table 3 CIs are asymmetric or truncated.

our_assessment.why: Recomputed from the deposit; the change column cross-checks it.

checked.how: efetch XML -> body text (abstract + body) read in full; tables via tools/jats2txt.py --tables
checked.result: Author manuscript, not the typeset article; the Open Practices statement is not in it. Europe PMC fullTextXML -> HTTP 500 (known trap).

Analysed sample only (104 of 112; the explicit-only baseline n is not deposited, which may explain the satisfaction baseline mismatch 42.47 vs 42.18). One covariate outlier: T1 implicit evaluation of strangers 2715.9.

datasheet.composition: one row per spouse: couple and person IDs, sex, implicit self/partner/stranger indices and orientation RTs at T1/T2, explicit self-esteem, satisfaction, partner evaluation at T1/T2, Big Five, attachment, depression
datasheet.caveats: Item-level and trial-level priming data not deposited, so per-session reliability of the implicit indices cannot be estimated.

relations.why: Item 8 of mark's blinded known-answer control of the reading protocol.

open_questions: Unblinding (mark, known_answer_control): my call before unblinding -- key analysis reproduces; Tables 2-3 carry reporting errors (pasted cell, d column, CIs); the claim is not distinguishable from a residualised-change artefact. Checked-type defects: moderate.
With trial-level priming data, per-session split-half reliability of the self and partner indices would pin down the null model's parameters instead of fitting them to four correlations.
